newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian premier keeps pressure on Kohl over euro.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian premier keeps pressure on Kohl over euro.

text.p: Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber on Sunday continued his vocal campaign against a softening of the entry criteria for Europe's single currency, urging German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to delay the project if the criteria were not met.
"If the requirements are not fulfilled then, of course, we will have to agree on a thorough, controlled postponement," Stoiber told the weekly Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
"The criteria determine the timetable and not the other way around," he told German Radio.

Stoiber is a senior member of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) which is a partner in Kohl's Bonn coalition. As the premier of Germany's largest state, he has great power to influence the national debate.

"If you say that the euro must come on January 1, 1999 as agreed and basically no longer say the criteria determine the timetable, then of course you create the impression that the criteria are considered less important than the timetable," he said.
By calling for a potential delay of monetary union, Stoiber has opened a huge rift with Kohl and his Christian Democrats (CDU), the CSU's larger sister party.
He urged Kohl to make clear he does not agree with CDU members who have suggested weakening the criteria rather than risk a postponement of EMU.
"The chancellor has not done this but he should stand up to these voices," Stoiber told Welt am Sonntag.
The Maastricht treaty on European Union defines a range of economic targets that would-be participants must meet in 1997 to qualify for the single currency in 1999.

Among the most important is the goal of limiting public budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, a target which France has said it is not likely to meet and Germany is struggling to fulfil.
Because of the risk that key EU members could narrowly miss the deficit target, a discussion is raging over how strictly to interpret the three percent target.

Stoiber told German Radio if the criteria were not strictly observed he would vote against German membership of monetary union when the issue was debated in the upper house of parliament, representing the federal states.

In a series of high profile interviews over the past week, Stoiber has repeatedly insisted that the German parliament agreed in 1992 to back monetary union (EMU) only on condition that the euro is as strong as the mark.
"That cannot have been right in 1992 and then be wrong in 1997," he said.
Kohl himself warned against a delay last week, saying it would upset financial markets and risk the failure of the ambitious project altogther.

Stoiber called such doomsday scenarios "absurd" and warned instead of the consequences of giving up the strong German currency for a weak euro union if the budget criterion were not strictly observed.

"If you veer from this you will undoubtedly destroy trust in the stability of the euro with all the subsequent consequences: a weak euro against the dollar and all the consequences that would result," he said.
Stoiber dismissed those who say his campaign for strict interpretation of the criteria is an attempt to raise his own political profile ahead of Bavarian state elections in 1998.
"Whoever insinuates I am doing this only because of a state election is suggesting that you cannot win an election with a pro-euro policy, and has already given up on the general election," he said.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
